questions.q: What is the formula for calculating a downtime budget from an availability percentage, per this lesson?
options: downtime = (1 − availability) × total time
downtime = availability × total time
downtime = total time ÷ availability
downtime = availability + total time
questions.explain: The allowed downtime is the fraction of time the system is permitted to be down, which is (1 − availability) multiplied by the total period.

questions.q: Roughly how much downtime per year does 99.99% availability allow?
options: About 52.6 minutes
About 8.76 hours
About 3.65 days
About 5.26 minutes
questions.explain: 99.99% ("four nines") allows about 52.6 minutes of downtime per year — 5.26 minutes is the figure for 99.999%.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe each additional nine of availability as an order-of-magnitude jump rather than a linear cost increase?
options: Because each nine typically requires a fundamentally different architecture — e.g. moving from manual response to real automatic failover — not just incremental effort
Because SQL Server licensing costs increase by exactly 10x per nine
Because each nine actually allows 10x more downtime, not less
Because the math is only an approximation and isn't really meaningful
questions.explain: Getting from 99.9% to 99.99% usually requires real automatic failover technology rather than manual intervention — a categorically different level of engineering, not a small tweak.

questions.q: Why can't a human reliably hit a 99.99% availability target through manual failover alone, per this lesson?
options: Because 99.99% only allows about 52.6 minutes of downtime across the entire year, and manual detection-and-failover time per incident can easily exceed that budget over multiple incidents
Because manual failover is technically impossible in SQL Server
Because 99.99% doesn't require any failover at all
Because humans are not allowed to operate SQL Server under an SLA
questions.explain: 52.6 minutes a year is a very small budget; a handful of manual failovers taking many minutes each would exceed it, so automatic failover is typically required.

questions.q: A stakeholder wants "99.99% uptime, same as now" on a standalone SQL Server instance with ~30-minute manual failovers per incident. What does the nines math say?
options: It's not achievable as-is — even two such incidents in a year would exceed the ~52.6-minute annual downtime budget for 99.99%
It's already achievable with no changes, since 30 minutes is a short outage
99.99% allows unlimited downtime as long as failover eventually happens
Standalone instances automatically qualify for 99.999% availability
questions.explain: With only ~52.6 minutes of allowed downtime per year, two 30-minute manual failover incidents already exceed the budget — the current setup can't deliver that target without real automatic failover.
